title: Breathing Deeply, Master Zhiyi's Meditation Instructions
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The teacher emphasizes that true understanding of Buddhist teachings and practices requires a deep study and practice of meditation techniques, including breathing exercises like counting breaths. Simply memorizing enough to overcome obstacles is not enough; one must also cultivate a profound understanding of the scriptures and develop a genuine connection with their own mind and body through consistent practice. By doing so, practitioners can access deeper states of consciousness and gain new insights into the nature of reality.

sentences.text: Alright, well, it's always good to hear these things again, for the recording and for our sanity.
Isn't it crazy?
You're sitting there, even though we barely started, you're tired, and the teacher reads some obscure Zen thing, and you're supposed to get what he just said, or she just said.
It's ridiculous, so third time is good.
*Book of Serenity Case 3, Invitation of the Patriarch of Eastern India.
Naraja of an East Indian country invited the 27th Buddhist Patriarch Prajnatara to a feast.
Naraja asked him, why don't you read scriptures?
Patriarch said, this poor wayfarer doesn't dwell in the realms of body or mind when breathing in, doesn't get involved in myriad circumstances when breathing out.
I always reiterate such a scripture, hundreds, thousands, millions of scrolls.*

In his commentary, Wan Song, the Chinese teacher who compiled this book, tells a brief story of Prajnatara's life, which is not unusual in these, and includes a wonderful little part about how, as a boy, Prajnatara remembered a past life in which he and his teacher, whom he was just meeting in this life, practiced deeply together.
So his teacher knew they were destined to practice together.
His teacher, pretty quick, I guess, ordained him and gave him the name Prajnatara, which is a really big deal name.
Prajna is the same Prajna that we think of: transcendent wisdom, wisdom beyond any idea of wisdom.
And Tara is a jewel, so the jewel of wisdom.
Interestingly, Wan Song doesn't mention Prajnatara's other claim to fame, which is that he was Bodhidharma's teacher.
I guess he just figures we all knew that.
So we have this teacher talking about breath practice.
We can relate to that.
Next in the classical koan collection is a little poem by another teacher, earlier than Wan Song, who we think gathered these stories together in just a little simple verse commentary.
It's not such an elaborate book.
This is someone named Tian Tong.
So here's Tian Tong's verse about this story of Prajnatara's breath practice.
*A cloud rhino gazes at the moon, its light engulfing radiance.
A wood horse romps in spring, swift and unbridled.
Under the eyebrows a pair of cold blue eyes.
How can reading scriptures reach the [unclear: "piercing of oxide"]?
The clear mind produces vast eons.
Heroic power smashes the double enclosure.
In the subtle round mouth of the pivot turns the spiritual works.
Wan Song forgot the road by which he came.
Shide led him back by the hand.*
So probably I should have a handout and read that quite a few times right now.
Remember any of that?

These poems are just packed with allusion and meaning and references to old stories, and some of the meanings are actually in the sound and the shapes of the characters, which is lost to me reading it in English translation.
But Wan Song, the later guy who put this together, does comment on it in detail, kind of like a couplet at a time.
I think it's the first couplet that concerns us here, the one that said, "A cloud rhino gazes at the moon, its light engulfing radiance.
A wood horse romps in spring, swift and unbridled."
So this is very symbolic and tangible, right?
We have rhinos in the clouds.
We have the moon engulfing the light radiance of that moon.
We have a horse.
I don't know why it's a wood horse, but it's a wood horse to challenge our conceptions, maybe, of what a horse is.
But it's romping, it's swift, unbridled, free.
So Wan Song helps us connect the dots here.
He says the cloud rhino, gazing at the moon, its light engulfing radiance, is from an ancient Chinese song that invokes inhaling.
Maybe that moment of amazement, right?
We see something.
We tend to inhale.
Look up and you see something beautiful, that first moment of recognition.
It's like something entering with the life breath.
Inspiration, same root there as respiration.
In the song, or some story that came before the song, this is 5,000 years of literary history we got to play with, the cloud rhino was so inspired that he grew his horn.
So you really get inspired as you breathe in.
In our story, Prajnatara says that one doesn't dwell in the realms of body or mind when breathing in.
Not dwelling.
So something beyond the body and mind.
Through the body and mind, for sure.
No body and mind, no breath.
We're also in the clouds.
That inspired.
Not caught in here.
So, cloud rhino breathing in.
Wood horses romping in the spring is more obvious, isn't it?
Swift, unbridled.
I didn't say it very well, but you know what I mean.
Wood horses do.
They're fired up.
So this is the exhale.
And the horse, wildly gallivanting around, is not caught by fences or boundaries or shoulds.
The horse is wild and free.
Unbridled, right?
So the bridle is what we put on ourselves to make ourselves, I don't know what, go to work or something.
Be who we're supposed to be according to some idea we have, some idea we have of what we think everyone else's idea of us is, right?
So we can measure up properly and suffer our whole lives.
So, free from the suffering of being me, which is completely being me.
Then Wan Song goes on to say, yeah, this whole thing really is important about the breathing, that we should study this very deeply.
Wan Song writes:
*The Sanskrit word anapana is translated as breathing out and breathing in.
And there are six methods involved with this.
Counting, following, stopping, contemplating, returning, and purification.
The details are in the great treatise on cessation and contemplation by the master of Tiantai.
Those whose preparation is not sufficient should not fail to be acquainted with this.*
So in this little case about not studying old books and just breathing, our commentator says, you better study this old book about breathing to really understand breathing.
Fair enough.
Because we start out just with our idea, our half-formed idea.
So the old book he's talking about, by the master of Tiantai, is by the sixth-century Chinese teacher, Xi, Xi, which is a challenging name for English speakers and hard for me to say.
It's a whole little pile of vowel sounds with a soft Z at the beginning.
In Pinyin, Z-H-I-Y-I, Z-H-I-Y-I, Xi.
In the earlier Wade-Giles, it was, sorry, that was Z, here it's Z, C-H-I-H-I.
Anyway, I mention all that because I first learned about this from Norman, 15, 20 years ago, and I can never remember the name of the guy, so I could never look it up.
It took me another decade or two for it to come around again, which is fine, there's other things to do in the meantime.
There's way more teachings out there than we'll ever get to in this lifetime, even though only a fraction of them are translated into English.
So Master Xi is actually an important ancestor in a different school of Buddhism than Zen, or Chan, as it's called in China.
It's an ancestor in the Tendai Buddhist tradition.
But remember, our great ancestor Dogen started there, so we don't have to worry if we're a little hung up on sectarianism, which might be more our problem than anybody else's, I don't know.

Dogen ordained in that school at the Tendai headquarters on Mount Hiei above Kyoto, and several of us last year and other years as well have gotten to go to that very spot, the very building where that happened.
So Dogen definitely would have known about Master Xi and his teachings.
Xi is mostly known for his fabulous and long writings, and I haven't really studied them more than the Wikipedia summary, about subtle things, full of philosophical stuff, rooted in the Lotus Sutra.
He was the first Lotus Sutra superfan.
And whole schools of Buddhism that studied the Lotus Sutra read him closely to this day.
But the cool thing about him is he wasn't just a scholar.
He was deeply a hands-on practitioner.
The evidence is clear in that, because unlike most of his contemporaries and later people in the tradition, he wrote with some depth about how to actually sit down and do this.
And he said you really need both together.
Deep study, deep practice.
Here's a famous thing he wrote:
*Understanding purifies practice.
Practice promotes understanding.
It's understanding like study.
Illuminating and enriching, guiding and penetrating.
They reciprocally beautify and embellish one another.
They are like the two hands on a single body, which, working together, keep it clean.*
Back to hand washing.
And he really drives this home.
There's a little more here.
He says it's not just a matter of learning enough to clear away the impediments and overcome in order to advance your own enlightenment.
That's not enough.
*You must achieve a thorough comprehension of the sutras and treatises so you can reveal to yourself and to others what none of you have heard before.*
So that's good, huh?
I'm not just like, study a little so I can go sit, have a clue what I'm doing.
You study deeply and you keep studying, just like you keep sitting.
So he wrote a lot about all the stuff you could study and was one of those great synthesizers.
Buddhism was even so vast in translation in China in the sixth century that I'm like, oh my god, I can't make sense of all this.
All these different strands and sutras and treatises, commentaries.
So periodically there have been great teachers who pulled it all together or tried to organize it.
None of us will probably get to that in this lifetime.
These folks really spent some time at it.
But like I say, what's cool about him is he also wrote meditation manuals, very detailed meditation manuals, which Wan Song says we should study to understand this case of Prajnatara.
And if it's in a koan, that means it's our business, the Zen business.
What's this really about?
On the surface it's like, yeah, sure, follow your breathing.
There must be more to it.

And the other thing that's odd is there's actually not that much written in our voluminous tradition, which ironically is always going around saying, don't rely on words and letters, and here's another big thick book to read.
But they also say, just sit.
You hear this, just sit.
I think Mr.
Yi is right.
There's a limit to that.
There's something about just sitting that's not just sitting.

We may need some new understanding to really just sit in a way that turns our life around and supports this beautiful suffering world in a way that we have never thought of before, never heard of before.
Not just an extension of the stuff we've accumulated, but some new clarity.
So anyway, she describes six kinds of practices, which she calls six dharma gates.
Six ways to orient yourself in zazen and also beyond it, which she writes about too.
One could study and lecture on this for many, many days, but I just get a couple shots at it, so I want to focus on the first one, the dharma gate of counting.
When I first started Zen practice, I was told, and maybe you were told too, okay, here's what to do.
Sit down, different ways to maybe arrange your legs, settle your posture, upright, open.
In my case, I learned just enough to get really stiff about it, to relax later.
And then, find your breathing in your belly, right, in your hara.
Notice the next exhalation and count it: one.
Inhale seems to happen somehow, a miracle, next exhalation: two.
You're right there with the breath: three.
Did I remember to turn on the dishwasher?
Oops, one.
Maybe you get to ten, back to one.
And that's all I heard.
Maybe there was more that I'd forgotten, if possible.
So, in my case, as a young man, I didn't know about any of the other options.
It's the only thing I knew about, the only practice I knew.

Maybe I could have looked around in the bookstore, it was before the internet, right, but I didn't know about any other kinds of things, like loving-kindness, or tonglen, or other ways of anchoring the attention.
I didn't know about all that.
Letting all that go and just being present, count.
I think on some level I must have appreciated that, something grounded about it.
Tangible, simple, seeming.
I think if I'd thought about it, I probably would have thought, well, gosh, this seems like some modern, made-up thing.
Maybe this is like a preparation for the real practice later.
Probably some teacher looked around in 1973 and said, these people are just spacing out, you need to give them something to do here.
I never would have imagined it was something like that, that it was being advocated, I think about 1,500 years ago, by this great ancestor in China.
So after some years I got kind of halfway good at it.
Some modest proportion of the time I could count pretty steadily from one to ten.
Sometimes I felt like I could count very accurately from one to ten and plan the next week.
And I said, well, this doesn't seem quite right, so I tried to sharpen my focus.
But eventually I did wonder.
It took me a while.
I don't know why, I'm more rebellious than other things, but in this I was not at all rebellious particularly, like, okay, this is my whole life now, count to ten.
But eventually I wondered, is there any other options?
And I was a new student at Tassajara Zen Monastery doing breath counting.

And Zenkay Blanch Hartman was the teacher, I think it was her first time teaching there, and she had recently become abbot of the Zen Center, which she had to be to lead the practice period at the great monastery.
So I went to her and described how, yeah, I'm pretty good at this, is there anything else to do?
Should I just keep doing this?
She peered at me and said, yeah, I know what you mean.
We learned how to count from one to ten from childhood.
Easily can get a little automatic.
So now I'm on the edge of my seat, and she said, why don't you count down from ten to one?
And I knew enough to just say, okay, thank you.
Depart.
And I'd be like, oh, really?
Come on!
Give me something better, man.
So I did that for a number of years.
Ten, nine, it's less automatic, right?
You should try it.
Oh, eight, okay, I better go back to ten.
Here's how Master Ji writes about it in his meditation manual:
*The six Dharma gates to the sublime and how powerful it is.
First counting is the gate to the sublime.
Through relying on counting the breaths, the practitioner gains the ability to manifest the first four jhanas, the four immeasurable minds, and the four formless absorptions.*
So something deep actually can be happening here.
And I did start noticing, as I soldiered on at Tassajara at that time, some sense of being more grounded, more present.
Sometimes things seemed a little different than usual in body and mind.
I thought, oh, that's interesting, different things happening.
But I never then, or particularly now, studied these particular things that he's talking about that we can gain the ability to manifest.
But maybe they were manifesting in some way.
The four jhanas, the four immeasurable minds, the four formless absorptions.
And of course you can usually look this up.
The traditional Buddhist teaching is there's progressive states of deep concentration and they're important.
There's another one where the language gets a little confusing.
Mostly you hear about them in the Pali voicing, which is with the j, jhana, J-H-A-N-A, jhana.
Your vipassana buddies would call them the jhanas.
But the Sanskrit edition is more of a da sound than a ja sound, so it gets romanized with a d, dhyana, D-H-Y-A-N-A.
Dhyana.
These states, more and more settled, quieter and quieter.
Peaceful, but with particular characteristics.
I'm in this one, or I'm in that one.
The third one, the second one.
And then, interestingly for our fate here as Zen students, the character the Chinese chose to translate this as, this jhana, is chan.
In the Chinese, Chan; Zen in the Japanese.
So we are literally all about this thing that we don't know about.
Or maybe we know about it in a deep, felt way, or maybe we don't recognize all the categories.
Maybe some of us do.
Mostly, in our school, we treasure all this, but we don't get too excited about it.
It's kind of our plan.
Our school tends to be a little dismissive sometimes, which gives us some flak from the more traditional schools.
Don't get lost in steps and stages, we would say.
And there's some wisdom there, because we're so dang good at making everything a project, right?
Once it's a project, we have to do it right.
And already embedded in there, though we didn't even notice, was me and the project.
That me is definitely inadequate to the project.
But somehow you're all stubborn enough to keep trying, right?
And sometimes we feel like, oh, I'm making a little progress, and we get excited.
My old teacher Blanche has a famous story about that too, which she told us, I think, multiple times that practice period.
We made a lovely little book of her teachings and it's in there too.
She started getting pretty settled into this breath counting, because she got the same instruction, apparently.
I don't know if she knew any other options when I went to see her.
I was only a couple of years into her practice, I believe.
If I understand the timeline right, she started at Berkeley in the early 70s with Norman and Kathy and other people we know.
She moved over to San Francisco, so she got to practice with Suzuki Roshi somewhere towards the end of his life.
Maybe the last year that he was active, I'm not sure.
Look carefully, because the timelines never quite line up.
Memory.
But anyway, she felt very bewildered for some time, lost in thought and distracted, and thought, this is not for me.
Blanche would always talk a lot about how self-conscious she would feel.
She was a bunch older than all the young hippies who were getting into this, and felt a little out of step with them.
She figured this was one more aspect of that: they're getting it, I'm not getting it.
But then after a while, she had a very beautiful posture.
You never get to see her sitting, but there's a nice picture of that in the front of the book.
Very serene.
Very grounded, actually.
I'm sure that went way back.
So she started feeling easier.
Maybe if she knew about these eight stages, she thought she was at 1.3 or something.
So she went to Suzuki Roshi and said something like, "Roshi, I'm really happy.
I'm starting to get a hang of this.
I can stay with my breathing and posture."
And Suzuki Roshi cut her off, in apparently a very stern voice.
I don't know if he was quite yelling, but a strong, strong voice, to say, "You don't do zazen.
Zazen does zazen."
Ding-a-ling-a-ling, bye.
She made a big impression, as you can imagine, especially someone like all of us who feels challenged, a little caught by conditioning around insecurity.
Like, okay, I just got a big smackdown, I don't get it.
What?
Something to chew on.
I was talking about Blanche the other night in Bellingham, and she gave me a few little things to chew on in a similar way.
Pissed me off, argued with, and had to think about for years.
So I guess she never stopped thinking about this saying from Suzuki Roshi.
So we're a little leery there.
It's the point of that little sidebar about doing it right.
It's a problem, trying to do it right, because we only have this subjective mind trying to figure out if we're opening to the unconditioned.
Are there right marks here?
I read about it in the book.
Gee, guys, I'm supposed to read the books, what's wrong with you?
What are you supposed to do?
Does it even matter?
Seems like it does.
Suzuki Roshi did teach breath counting.
This was collected in *Not Always So*, the second collection of his teachings, heavily edited later by his students, and there's a third one coming out soon.
But anyway, he said something like:
*You may think it's silly to count your breath from one to ten, losing track of your count, starting over.
If you just used a computer, pretty good in 1960, whatever, computer.
If you just used a computer, there would not be any mistake.
But the underlying spirit is quite important.
While we are counting each number, we find that our life is limitlessly deep.
To count each breath is to breathe with our whole mind and body.
We count each number with the power of the whole universe.
So when you really experience counting your breath, you will have deep gratitude.
You will not be interested in something just because it is considered great, or uninterested in something usually considered to be small.*
So that sounds just like what Prajantaro was saying.
Remember how he was saying in the case, *I don't dwell in the realms of body and mind breathing in.
I don't get involved in varied circumstances when breathing out.* There's a freedom there, isn't there?
And then the last part is significant and points right back to counting.
He says, *I always reiterate such a scripture, hundreds, thousands of millions of scrolls.* Just keep breathing.
Just keep counting.
It's not you breathing and counting.
It's just breathing and counting.
Counting, breathing, breathing, counting.
I don't have time to share it, but if you ever read the great little biography of Suzuki Roshi, *Crooked Cucumber*, I recommend re-reading it.
It's a really great book.
David Chadwick recalls that at one point Suzuki Roshi actually almost drowned in Tassajara Creek.
And he was really upset with himself that he kind of lost his composure.
He didn't just calmly go to his fate or something.
Zen, you know, sometimes.
And so how did he respond to that?
He went back to breath counting in his own practice and told everybody, do breath counting.
To really ground ourselves in our practice.
So that's what I'm going to boldly recommend to us today.
If you've never done breath counting, why don't you take it up?
Try it out, deeply.
Give it some time and space.
If it's far in the rear view, and you tell stories in Dharma talks about how you used to do that back when you were young and foolish, do it again.
I will take my own advice.
Because G goes on to say this is not an introductory practice.
He starts there, wisely, I think.
I started there.
Many of us start there.
But he explains that every one of the six gates completely includes the whole universe.
Completely includes the other gates.

And rather than leaving you totally hanging, being a total jerk about this, I'll tell you a little about the second Dharma gate, and then a little bit of advice from Master G about monitoring our mind during practice.
So eventually you too may feel a little stale about breath counting.
Not just because you think you have it down.
That's kind of a false marker, that's what I have learned.
"I have it down" doesn't mean you have it down.
It's a subjective thing.
There's a deep settledness and freedom.
Counting the breath is just a joy.
But the numbers just don't really seem, I think, we need those anymore.
They just drift off.
And then you naturally, maybe, find yourself in the second Dharma gate, which is following.
Following the breath.
Or maybe because you're too stubborn to do breath counting for 30 minutes, you just start there.
You let it gradually, gradually, gradually fade into silence.
Each number is quieter and quieter and quieter.
And in the counting itself, it's not really about the number anyway.
It's not exactly just about the breath either.
But conventionally we can say it's about the breath.
Subtle, subtle feelings.
Myriad, infinite feelings.
Every breath is subtly different, and rich in movement and shift and temperature.
Expansion and release and flow.
It's not just happening where you imagine your airways to be either, right?
It's your whole body.
Your whole body is breathing.
Breathing you.
And the counting is a support to really showing up.
But maybe the counting gets quieter and quieter and quieter until you can't exactly hear it, but you feel its resonance.
You feel the space of counting without the actual counting.
We're following.
Master G says:
*As for the cultivation of following, one relinquishes the previous Dharma of counting, and relies single-mindedly on following the coming in and going out of the breath.
The mind abides in the conditions associated with the breath.*
Meaning everything.
All the conditions, right?
All the feelings.
Conditions associated with the breath.
Freeing, remaining, and you are free of any distraction or scattering of your point of attention.
You're just right here.
And so, just like Suzuki Roshi's connection to Blanche, not to think "I am following the breath," because then you're not following.
It's not this practice of following when you think "I am following the breath."
Don't think "I am counting the breath," because then you're not doing the practice of counting.
It's just counting.
Following does following.
Counting does counting.
And just like you did with counting, he tells you about how great this is going to be.
Don't get attached to this stuff.
He writes:
*As the mind becomes fine and subtle, it becomes peaceful, still and free of disorder.
One becomes aware of the breath.*
Like deeply aware of the breath.
*The breath is now long.
The breath is short.
The breath is pervading the body.
The breath is coming in.
The breath is going out.
The mind and the breath carry on in a state of mutual interdependence.*
We don't know where the mind stops and the breath starts.
There's no such distinction.
*And the movement of the mind becomes tranquil and settled into a state of stillness.*
That sounds good.
So he described all six of these gates in great detail.
It's really cool getting into it.
And he also wrote a companion volume, for general points about meditation.
You can also apply it to all of this.
It's layers and layers and layers, and very specific.
It's very cool.
And like any ancient translated text, you quickly get confused and have to reread three times and make an outline and all this.
But it's actually pretty clear.
So there's a whole chapter in this companion volume about monitoring and course correcting, which is good for us.
Because again, we may misunderstand just sitting.
I think, I'll just plunk myself down and whatever happens happens and the bell rings.
I wonder what happens.
We don't want to just put it in park.
We don't necessarily want to put it in drive either.
Don't put it in park.
So there's some creative course correcting done in this gentle, wholesome spirit.
So he has five or six points, but I just want to share two of them and then I'll close the talk.
Thanks for listening to all this stuff.
Two of the states that you can correct for are called sinking and floating.
I think you already know what he's about there.
Sinking and floating.
So, sinking: dull, distracted, which is how he describes it.
What constitutes sinking?
*If one is sitting, one's mental state is murky and dim, one doesn't remember anything, or if one's head tends to droop downwards.*
So this is a very long tradition of falling asleep in the meditation hall.
Thousands of years old.
*One's head tends to droop downwards.
This constitutes the marks of sinking.*
So that's sinking.
What should you do about it?
We'll come back to that.
Let's look at floating first.
So floating.
I think we know what he means there, too.
Wow.
He wrote:
*What are the indicators of floating?
If while one is sitting, the mind prefers to drift off and move about, the body, too, is ill at ease, uncomfortable, maybe even pain.

It is appropriate at such a time to stabilize the mind by directing it downwards and anchoring it at the navel.* [unclear: "Nara."] *Thus controlling chaotic thinking, the mind then abides in stability.
It's easy to establish the mind in stillness when you do this.*
So that sounds like that was an instruction again.
What I was told at the very beginning: bring my awareness to the belly.
Feel the breath there.
One.
So we already have deeply internalized, I think, the antidote to floating.
So we don't need much help there.
But the problem is maybe we're too good at it, and we spend a lot of time sinking.
So here's what he suggests for sinking:
*At such a time when you're sinking, one should anchor one's mindfulness at the tip of the nose and compel one's mind,*
invite one's mind,
*to abide in the midst of conditions,*
the feeling right there,
*so that there's no breaking up and scattering of the mental focus.*
For sinking, bring your awareness up.
Floating, bring your awareness down.
Simple, right?
It's really simple.
Not so easy to do, because we're so habituated and semi-conscious half the time, just doing this all by rote and habit.

So that's why I'm pushing and cheering us on to renew breath awareness, because it really gives you a kind of place to practice, a space to explore floating and sinking and every other possible state we can imagine.
Isn't that good?
And again, your Vipassana buddies might be like, yeah, we've been putting tension in our nostrils forever.
You didn't know about that?
So play with that.
Just offer this very gentle, counteractive energy.
Just going to gently move the energy up, energy down.
Breath in the belly, breath in the nose.
But it's still just one breath, right?
Just one body.
Just one moment.
And every breath, body, moment is completely new and unexpected, actually.
We think it's just me breathing, or now I'm good at counting, or blah, blah, blah.
You can picture Suzuki Roshi chewing the Blanche out.
We've lost the thread.
It's okay.
Of course.
What do you think is going to happen?
Start again.
Start again.
Sesshin is not about solving our problems, reviewing our life, or making a plan, really.
That will happen.
Of course it will.
The possibility here is much deeper than that.
Especially because we get to do this all day and all night.
So the last thing I want to say for now is, don't be fooled by conventional time or our schedule.
We had to put on there, zazen starts at this time.
Ding, ding, ding.
Zazen ends at that time.
Ding.
So we can stay coordinated.
But it's not really true.
So sorry.
Sorry for that.
Zazen never ends.
The bells are just part of your practice, like everything else.
Part of our practice.
And since zazen never ends, zazen never begins.
It's not something that begins or ends.

Oh, finally.
